newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe business, unions seek end to strike wave.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe business, unions seek end to strike wave.

text.p: Zimbabwe trade unions have started talks with the country's key private business sector to try to stop an annual wave of pay strikes which they say is undermining productivity and clouding the national investment climate.

Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) Secretary-General Morgan Tsvangirayi told Reuters that the discussions, which began early this month, would culminate in a national conference on wages and working conditions to be held at the end of June.
"These are not ordinary run-off-the-mill talks," he said.

"They are concrete and a very serious attempt to restore industrial stability, to secure job security, to maintain and improve shop-floor productivity and of course ensure that there is fair renumeration in industry".

The June 30 conference is jointly organised by the ZCTU -- whose membership includes workers in the vital mining, tourism, agriculture, telecommunications and manufacturing sectors -- and the Employers Confederation of Zimbabwe (EMCOZ).

Zimbabwe has this year been rocked by a series of short wildcat strikes -- which have become an annual ritual -- from workers seeking to strengthen their negotiating positions for higher wage rises for the financial year starting next month.
Sectors which have been disrupted include banking, textiles and clothing, transport, hotels and restaurants. Workers have been demanding annual pay increases of between 25 and 60 percent.

EMCOZ executive director Peter Kunjeku and Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) chief executive Joe Foroma said wage rises must be negotiated against the performance of specific sectors or sub-sectors.

"It is not possible to benchmark minimum increases because the performances are different," Foroma said of a general demand that 1997 pay rises must be around 24 percent, three percentage points above Zimbabwe's current inflation rate.
Zimbabwe's agriculture-powered economy is expected to grow by around six percent this year after a seven percent rise in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996.
Kunjeku said EMCOZ welcomed the ZCTU's commitment to finding a lasting solution to the creeping industrial unrest.
"We are getting into this to address some very fundamental issues: Jobs can only be guaranteed and secured if production is higher and sustained," he said.
Both Tsvangirayi and Kunjeku said this was a priority.

"The economy can only grow if we realise increased investment, both local and foreign and we need stability for that," the ZCTU boss said, saying the unions were aware unrest undermined the investment climate.
"But we are also glad our partners realise that industry must pay decent wages and improve working conditions to get what we are all aiming for," he said.
"We are talking to improve mutual trust, to lay the basis for collective bargaining for both working conditions and salaries. We must also agree on a way of resolving disputes," Tsvangirayi said.
